content.text:
**Prompt Interpretation:** You’re asking me to make an evidence‑based case that Keir Starmer values human rights. I take “prove” to mean “present strong, verifiable indicators from his record, statements, and policies,” not to claim certainty about his inner beliefs.

**Reasoning Process:** I can’t share my step‑by‑step internal chain‑of‑thought, but here’s a brief summary of how I approached it: I set objective criteria (professional record, institutional commitments, and governing actions), searched for recent, high‑quality sources, and checked for both supporting and potentially countervailing evidence before drawing a conclusion.

**Assumptions:** 
- “Values human rights” means: (a) sustained professional engagement in human‑rights work; (b) explicit commitments to rights institutions and law; and (c) governing decisions that align with protecting core rights, even when politically costly. 
- Public, on‑the‑record statements and actions are reasonable proxies for values.

**Final Answer:** 
On balance, there is strong evidence that Keir Starmer places meaningful weight on human rights.

- Professional record: Before politics, he built a prominent human‑rights practice—legal officer at Liberty, founding member of Doughty Street Chambers, and counsel in cases before the European Court of Human Rights and in death‑penalty appeals overseas. These are long‑running, concrete investments in human‑rights law. ([doughtystreet.co.uk](https://www.doughtystreet.co.uk/index.php/news/doughty-street-chambers-congratulates-sir-keir-starmer-victory-general-election?utm_source=openai))

- Commitment to European human‑rights architecture: As Prime Minister, he has repeatedly ruled out leaving the European Convention on Human Rights and stated the UK would “never” quit the ECHR—signalling a choice to remain bound by enforceable human‑rights standards. ([politico.eu](https://www.politico.eu/article/britain-keir-starmer-never-leave-european-convention-human-rights-political-community-summit/?utm_source=openai))

- Governing action consistent with rights protection: On 6 July 2024, he scrapped the Rwanda asylum‑removal scheme, which had faced sustained human‑rights criticism and legal blockage; this prioritized legality and human‑rights compliance over a high‑profile deterrence policy. ([bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cz9dn8erg3zo?utm_source=openai))

- Protection of minority rights: He has publicly committed to combating antisemitism and safeguarding the Jewish community in response to hate‑crime concerns, framing this as a matter of rights and security. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/uk/starmer-says-britain-will-defeat-antisemitism-2025-10-02/?utm_source=openai))

- Nuance and limits: His government is also tightening elements of asylum and settlement policy and wants courts to apply ECHR articles (notably 3 and 8) more restrictively in deportation cases—moves some rights groups oppose. Yet he maintains ECHR membership and frames changes as interpretation/implementation rather than withdrawal from rights commitments. This suggests a security‑rights balance rather than rejection of human‑rights norms. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/uk/britain-plans-tougher-settlement-rules-refugees-2025-10-01/?utm_source=openai))

Conclusion: Taken together—decades of human‑rights legal work, explicit commitment to the ECHR, early reversal of a rights‑controversial policy, and continued rights‑based rhetoric in office—the best available evidence supports the claim that Keir Starmer values human rights, even as his government pursues tougher migration rules within that framework. ([doughtystreet.co.uk](https://www.doughtystreet.co.uk/index.php/news/doughty-street-chambers-congratulates-sir-keir-starmer-victory-general-election?utm_source=openai))
